summary: Dat Ngo, an AI architect at Arize AI, presents on observability, evaluation, and experimentation for non-deterministic AI systems. He works with the world's largest enterprises and estimates having processed between 100 billion and 1 trillion tokens last year. The talk addresses three pillars: observability (what is happening in your system), evals (deriving signal from systems), and managing improvements in a world where fixes can introduce hidden regressions. Arize's approach is built on OpenTelemetry, providing auto-instrumentation through a single line of code that generates traces and spans as audit records. Ngo emphasizes that code does not audit agents or harnesses—telemetry does. Beyond individual traces, observability encompasses sessions (back-and-forth conversation state), distributional views showing all possible agent paths, branches, and loops, plus real-time analytics dashboards. A key example illustrates trajectory-level observability: an agent called tool B before tool A when B depended on A, a mismatch invisible in code review but caught through telemetry. Five flavors of evaluation signal are identified: LLM as a judge, human feedback, golden datasets, deterministic checks, and business metrics. Eval scopes range from single-span to multi-span to trajectory to session-level. Ngo stresses finding the minimal set of evals due to associated costs. The experimentation pillar covers changes to prompts, models, orchestration, and configurations, testable via UI or programmatically. Data can come from collected traces or direct upload of input-output pairs. Arize exposes all primitives via CLI and tools for coding agents. The company's stated goal is to automate users out of the entire observability-eval-experimentation flywheel through Alex, an AI layer that scans traces, surfaces high latency and errors, and creates evals automatically. Two products exist: Arize Phoenix (open source, single container, no Kubernetes) and Arize AX (enterprise, used by Uber, Booking, Reddit).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Dat Ngo introduces himself as an AI architect at Arize AI working with large enterprises. He estimates processing 100 billion to 1 trillion tokens last year. The talk covers three topics: observability, evals, and managing improvements in a non-deterministic world where fixes can cause hidden regressions.

sections.title: Observability and OpenTelemetry
sections.summary: Arize is built on OpenTelemetry, enabling auto-instrumentation with one line of code. Traces and spans serve as audit records for agent behavior since code does not audit agents—telemetry does. This foundation supports any framework or SDK setup.

sections.title: Sessions and Distributional Views
sections.summary: Observability extends to sessions (back-and-forth conversation state) and distributional views showing all possible agent paths, branches, and loops. Trajectory evals can catch ordering issues like calling tool B before tool A when B depends on A. Analytics and customizable real-time dashboards remain valuable for enterprise users.

sections.title: Five Flavors of Eval Signal
sections.summary: Signal comes in five forms: LLM as a judge (tunable against golden datasets), human feedback (end-user satisfaction), golden datasets (trusted domain-expert labels), deterministic checks (schema and JSON validation), and business metrics (revenue, cost savings, time savings). Two personas emerge: technical users who build and automate, and domain experts who define evals and prompt engineering.

sections.title: Eval Scopes and Personas
sections.summary: Evals run at different scopes: single-span (one input/output), multi-span (data across multiple components), trajectory (full path correctness), and session-level (overall conversation quality and user state). Arize supports non-technical users running evals through UI-based model selection and template customization, while also allowing programmatic eval attachment for technical users.

sections.title: Experimentation and Improvement
sections.summary: Experimentation involves changes to prompts, models, orchestration, and configurations. Data can come from collected traces or direct upload of input-output pairs. Not everything needs evaluation—finding the minimal set of evals is important due to cost. Arize supports testing via UI or programmatically.

sections.title: Future Direction: Automation and Alex AI
sections.summary: Arize exposes all primitives via CLI, tools, and skills for coding agents. An AI system called Alex scans traces, surfaces high latency and errors, and creates evals automatically. The company's stated goal is to automate users out of the entire observability-eval-experimentation flywheel, making it feel like magic while not being magic.

sections.title: Products: Phoenix and AX
sections.summary: Arize offers two products: Arize Phoenix, which is open source and runs as a single container without Kubernetes, and Arize AX, the enterprise product used by Uber, Booking, and Reddit. Ngo closes and invites further conversation.
